chapters.name: Chapter 1: Getting the harvest in well

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Where harvests are lost, and why
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Walk your crop from field to buyer and mark where it loses quantity or value.
This lesson builds toward: For one crop, you will map its path from field to buyer and mark where it loses quantity or value, naming at least three loss points and what would fix them.
FAO estimated in 2019 that about 14 percent of the world's food is lost between harvest and the shop, before it ever reaches a market stall. On many African farms, losses for some crops are higher. Every bag lost is seed, fertilizer and work thrown away.
Losses happen at every step: harvesting too early or too late, leaving the crop in the rain, rough handling and bruising, heat, drying too slowly, insects such as weevils and the larger grain borer, rats, mould, and poor packing on bumpy roads. Some losses you can see (fewer bags); others you cannot (lower grade, lower price, or grain that is unsafe to eat).
The first step is to find your own biggest losses. Follow your crop from the field to the buyer and ask at each step: what goes wrong here, how much is lost, and what would it cost to fix?
Step by step:
- List each step your crop goes through: harvest, carry, dry, thresh or shell, store, pack, transport, sell.
- At each step, write what goes wrong (rain, bruising, insects, rats, mould).
- Estimate how much is lost or how much the price drops.
- Circle the two biggest losses; they are where you start.
Words to know:
- Post-harvest loss: food or value lost between harvest and sale.
- Larger grain borer: a beetle that bores into stored maize and cassava and turns it to powder.
- Grade: a quality class, such as first or second grade, that sets the price.
Official sources:
- FAO: Food loss and waste reduction (about 14 percent of food lost between harvest and retail, 2019)
Try it now: Draw your crop's path from field to buyer as a row of boxes. Under each box, write what goes wrong there and roughly how much is lost. Circle the two biggest losses.
You can now map where your harvest loses quantity or value and pick the losses to fix first.

check.q: Which insect is named as a storage pest that eats grain?
check.why: Weevils and the larger grain borer are storage insects that cause grain losses.

check.q: At the market, many of your tomatoes are rejected as crushed. What do you do?
options: Follow the crop back, find the step where crushing happens and what it would cost to fix
Sell to a different buyer next time and change nothing
check.why: Following the crop step by step shows where losses happen and what to fix.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Harvesting at the right time
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Identify the signs that each of your crops is ready and plan harvest days.
This lesson builds toward: For each of your crops, you will identify the signs that it is ready and plan harvest days with the forecast, with tools, bags or crates and labour ready before harvest.
Harvesting too early gives small, light grain or produce that will not ripen well; too late invites rain damage, insects, birds, theft and rot. Learn the signs for each crop.
Maize is mature when the husks are dry and the grain is hard with a black layer at its base; it can then dry further on the stalk for a short time if the weather is dry, but do not leave it out through rains. Beans and cowpea are ready when most pods are dry and rattle. Sorghum is ready when grain is hard and cannot be dented with a fingernail. Tomatoes are picked at the colour stage your buyer wants (often just turning colour for distant markets). Coffee: pick only red, ripe cherries. Tea: pluck the tender shoot, usually two leaves and a bud. Cassava roots spoil within a few days of harvest, so lift only what you can sell or process quickly.
Plan harvest days with the weather forecast. Harvest fresh produce in the cool early morning, keep it in the shade, and have bags, crates, tarpaulins and labour ready before you start.
Step by step:
- Write the ready signs for each crop you grow.
- Walk the field and check the signs each week as harvest nears.
- Check the forecast and pick dry days for grain.
- Have tarpaulins, bags or crates and labour ready.
- Harvest fresh produce in the cool morning and keep it in shade.
Words to know:
- Maturity: the stage when a crop is fully grown and ready to harvest.
- Black layer: a dark spot at the base of a maize grain that shows it is mature.
- Two leaves and a bud: the tender tea shoot that pluckers pick for good-quality tea.
Try it now: For two crops you grow, write the ready signs and the date you expect to harvest. Ask your buyer what stage or quality they want and write it down. Set a phone reminder to check the forecast a week before.
You can now tell when your crops are ready and plan harvest days that protect quality.

check.q: How do you know sorghum is ready to harvest?
options: The grain is soft and milky
The grain is hard and cannot be dented with a fingernail
check.why: Sorghum is ready when the grain is hard and cannot be dented with a fingernail.

check.q: Your maize is mature and heavy rain is forecast next week. What do you do?
options: Leave it on the stalk through the rains
Harvest before the rain, with tarpaulins and bags ready
Harvest only after the rains end
Cut it and leave it on the ground
check.why: Plan harvest with the forecast and do not leave mature maize out through rains.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Drying grain to a safe moisture
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Dry grain quickly and check that it has reached a safe moisture for storage.
This lesson builds toward: For freshly harvested grain, you will dry it quickly off the soil and check that it has reached a safe moisture, about 13 to 14 percent or the buyer's limit, checked with a meter or salt test.
Freshly harvested grain holds a lot of water. Damp grain heats up, moulds and attracts insects. FAO guidance on maize says drying it to a safe moisture of about 13 to 14 percent before mould grows is the most reliable way to prevent aflatoxin, and that drying should be fast: grain left damp for more than about two days is at much higher risk. Your buyer, cooperative or national standard may set its own maximum, so ask.
Dry on a clean tarpaulin, raised platform, mat or cement floor, never on bare soil. Spread grain thinly, turn it several times a day, and cover it or bring it in before rain and at night. Shelled grain dries faster than grain on the cob. Solar dryers, simple frames with a clear plastic cover, dry faster and keep out rain, dust and animals.
Check moisture before storage. The best tool is a moisture meter; cooperatives, buyers, extension offices and warehouses often have one. A rough home check is the salt test: put a handful of dry salt and some grain in a clean, dry glass bottle, shake for two to three minutes, and if salt sticks to the glass the grain is still too wet. Grain that passes can still be a little too damp, so confirm with a meter when you can.
Step by step:
- Harvest in dry weather.
- Spread grain thinly on a tarpaulin, mat, platform or cement, never on bare soil.
- Turn it several times a day; cover it from rain and at night.
- Dry fast: aim to reach a safe moisture within about two days of shelling.
- Do the salt test; confirm with a moisture meter at your cooperative or buyer.
- Store only when dry.
Words to know:
- Moisture content: how much water is in the grain, as a percentage of its weight.
- Moisture meter: a tool that measures grain moisture.
- Salt test: a rough home check: dry salt sticks to the bottle if grain is too wet.
- Solar dryer: a frame with a clear cover that uses the sun to dry crops faster and cleaner.
Official sources:
- FAO: Mycotoxin prevention and control in foodgrains: control of aflatoxin in maize
- FAO TECA/STI portal: Well dried maize benefits all: the solar maize dryer
Try it now: Do a salt test on a handful of your grain (or a neighbour's): dry bottle, dry salt, shake for two to three minutes, look at the glass. Then find out who near you has a moisture meter and the buyer's maximum moisture.
You can now dry grain fast on a clean surface and check it has reached a safe moisture before storage.

options: A frame with a clear plastic cover that dries grain faster and keeps out rain and dust
check.why: Solar dryers are simple frames with a clear cover that dry grain faster and protect it.

check.q: Rain clouds build in the afternoon while your shelled maize is drying outside. What do you do?
options: Leave it; it will dry later
Pour water off it after the rain
Cover it or bring it in before the rain
check.why: Cover grain or bring it in before rain and at night, so it does not get damp again.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Keeping the harvest safe and saleable

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Aflatoxin: what it is and how to prevent it
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Use the main steps that keep aflatoxin out of your maize and groundnuts.
This lesson builds toward: For maize, groundnuts or other at-risk crops, you will list and use the main steps that keep aflatoxin out, with mouldy and damaged grain sorted out and never eaten, sold or fed.
Aflatoxin is a poison made by certain moulds (Aspergillus) that grow on maize, groundnuts, sorghum and other crops, in the field and in storage. You often cannot see, smell or taste it. Eating it over time harms the liver and is linked to liver cancer and to stunted growth in children; large amounts can kill. It also passes from feed into milk and eggs. Buyers and national food standards bodies test for it and reject grain above the legal limit.
Prevention starts in the field: healthy crops, timely planting, and control of insects that damage cobs and pods. Harvest on time, do not leave the crop lying on the ground, and dry it fast to a safe moisture. FAO notes that aflatoxin levels in stored maize rise with weevil damage, so keep stores clean and insects out.
Sort before storing: remove mouldy, broken, discoloured, insect-damaged and shrivelled grains and cobs. Never eat, sell or feed animals mouldy grain. Biocontrol products such as Aflasafe, developed by IITA and registered in countries including Kenya, Nigeria and Ghana, are spread in the field before flowering to crowd out the toxic moulds; ask your extension officer or agro-dealer whether one is approved for your crop and area, and follow the label.
Step by step:
- Control insects that damage cobs and pods in the field.
- Harvest on time; do not leave the crop on the ground.
- Dry fast to a safe moisture.
- Sort out mouldy, broken, discoloured and insect-damaged grain.
- Store in clean, dry, insect-proof storage.
- Ask extension about an approved biocontrol product for your area.
Words to know:
- Aflatoxin: a poison made by some moulds on crops such as maize and groundnuts.
- Aspergillus: the group of moulds that can make aflatoxin.
- Biocontrol: using a harmless living organism to crowd out a harmful one.
- Sorting: picking out bad grains or produce by hand or machine.
Official sources:
- FAO: Mycotoxin prevention and control in foodgrains: control of aflatoxin in maize
- IITA: Aflasafe aflatoxin biocontrol products for Africa's farmers
Try it now: Take a sample of stored grain or groundnuts and sort it on a tray: separate mouldy, broken, discoloured and insect-damaged grains. Weigh or count them and write the share you removed. Write two steps you will change next season to reduce it.
You can now explain why aflatoxin is dangerous and use field, drying, sorting and storage steps to keep it out.

check.q: Which crops can aflatoxin moulds grow on?
check.why: Aspergillus moulds grow on maize, groundnuts, sorghum and other crops.

check.q: You find weevils in your stored maize. What do you do?
options: Ignore them; they do not matter
Feed the damaged grain to chickens
Sort out damaged grain and clean the store to keep insects out, because weevil damage raises aflatoxin
Mix the damaged grain with good grain
check.why: Aflatoxin levels rise with weevil damage; damaged grain is sorted out and never fed or sold.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Storing grain in hermetic bags
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Fill, seal and store a hermetic bag so insects die without chemicals.
This lesson builds toward: With dry, clean, sorted grain, you will fill, seal and store a hermetic bag, with each liner tied airtight and the bag off the floor, away from walls and safe from rats.
Hermetic means airtight. A hermetic bag, such as the PICS bag developed at Purdue University, has two inner plastic liners inside an outer woven sack. Once sealed, the insects and grain use up the oxygen inside and the insects die or stop breeding, with no insecticide. Purdue lists maize, sorghum, beans, cowpea, groundnut, rice and other crops as suited to the bags.
The bag only works if the grain is dry and the bag is airtight. Store only dry, clean, sorted grain. Fill the inner liner, push out as much air as you can, twist the neck and tie it tightly; then do the same with the second liner and finally the outer sack. Check for holes before use; a small hole lets air in and the bag stops working.
Keep bags off the floor on pallets or planks, away from walls, in a clean, dry, shaded store, and protect them from rats, which chew holes. Do not open them often: each opening lets in fresh air. Bags that are still whole can be reused next season. Other good options are metal silos and clean, raised, well-ventilated cribs for cobs.
Step by step:
- Check the grain is dry, clean and sorted.
- Check the bag liners for holes.
- Fill the inner liner, push out the air, twist and tie tightly.
- Tie the second liner, then the outer sack, the same way.
- Store on pallets, away from walls, in a dry, shaded, rat-proof store.
- Open only when needed; reuse bags that are still whole.
Words to know:
- Hermetic: airtight: no air can get in or out.
- Liner: a plastic bag inside the outer sack.
- Pallet: a wooden platform that keeps bags off the floor.
- Metal silo: a sealed metal bin for storing grain.
Official sources:
- Purdue University: Purdue Improved Crop Storage (PICS) hermetic bags
Try it now: Look at your store. Write three changes that would protect bags (pallets, gap from walls, rat-proofing, shade). If you can, buy one hermetic bag from an agro-dealer and practise tying each layer with dry grain.
You can now seal and store grain in hermetic bags so it keeps without chemicals.

check.q: What is inside the outer woven sack of a PICS bag?
check.why: A PICS bag has two inner plastic liners inside an outer woven sack.

check.q: You have filled and tied the first liner. What do you do next?
options: Push out air, twist and tie the second liner, then tie the outer sack
Leave the second liner open for air
Cut a hole to check the grain
check.why: Each liner and the outer sack is tied tightly so the bag stays airtight.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Keeping produce cool, grading and packing
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Keep fresh produce cool, grade it to the buyer's standard and pack it to arrive unbruised.
This lesson builds toward: For fresh produce, you will keep it cool, grade it to the buyer's standard and pack it to arrive unbruised, in clean, ventilated, labelled crates.
Fresh produce such as tomatoes, kale, mangoes and avocados keeps living and breathing after harvest. Heat speeds this up, so it ripens, wilts and rots faster. Harvest in the cool morning, keep produce in the shade at all times, and get it to the buyer quickly.
Without electricity, an evaporative cooler helps. The FAO-listed Zero Energy Cooling Chamber is a double brick wall with wet sand between the walls and a wet cover on top; as water evaporates it cools the inside and keeps the air moist so produce does not wilt. It works best in dry, hot places. Clay-pot coolers work the same way on a smaller scale.
Grading means sorting produce into classes by size, ripeness and quality, and taking out damaged items so they do not spoil the rest. Buyers pay more for even, clean, graded produce. Pack in clean, strong, ventilated crates rather than sacks for soft produce, do not overfill, and label each crate with the grade, date and your name. A phone photo of each graded batch helps settle disputes with buyers.
Step by step:
- Ask the buyer for their grades: size, ripeness, quality.
- Harvest in the cool morning and keep produce in shade.
- Sort into grades; remove damaged items.
- Use an evaporative cooler if you must hold produce.
- Pack in clean, ventilated crates; do not overfill.
- Label crates with grade, date and name; take a photo.
Words to know:
- Evaporative cooler: a store cooled by water evaporating from wet walls, sand or cloth.
- Grading: sorting produce into quality classes.
- Ventilated crate: a box with holes that lets air flow around produce.
Official sources:
- FAO TECA/STI portal: Zero Energy Cooling Chamber for vegetables
Try it now: Final task: write your one-page post-harvest plan for one crop. Put the buyer's quality rules at the top, then your harvest timing, drying and moisture check (for grain), aflatoxin steps, storage, and how you will cool, grade and pack.
You can now keep fresh produce cool, grade and pack it to the buyer's standard, and run a full post-harvest plan for one crop.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Buyer's rules and harvest timing No buyer's rules, or no signs of readiness. The buyer's quality rules are at the top, with the signs of readiness and how harvest days will be planned. Shows tools, bags or crates and labour booked before harvest. Drying and moisture No drying surface or moisture check (for grain). Drying off the soil, turning and covering, and a moisture check with a meter or salt test. Names where a moisture meter can be used, such as a cooperative or buyer. Aflatoxin prevention No steps against aflatoxin, or mouldy grain is kept. Field, drying, sorting and store steps, with mouldy grain removed and never eaten, sold or fed. Asks extension whether an approved biocontrol product fits the crop and area. Storage Storage method missing, or grain stored damp. Dry, clean, sorted grain in hermetic bags or another good store, off the floor and safe from rats. Notes how often bags will be checked without opening them. Cooling, grading and packing Fresh produce in sacks or sun, or no grading. Cool harvest times, shade, grading to the buyer's standard, and clean ventilated crates with labels. Uses an evaporative cooler or photos of each graded batch. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part of the plan and check it again.

check.q: Where does a Zero Energy Cooling Chamber work best?
check.why: Evaporative coolers work best in dry, hot places, where water evaporates fast.

check.q: A buyer says your crates were the wrong grade. What helps settle the dispute?
options: Labels with grade and date, and a phone photo of each graded batch
check.why: Labelled crates and a photo of each graded batch help settle disputes with buyers.
